summary: This memo extends NNTP so a client and server can use Transport Layer Security. The main goal is encrypting a single link for confidentiality, with data integrity, optional certificate-based authentication and optional compression also possible. It was later updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: Reading newsgroups used to be like shouting across a room. This lets the reader and the news server whisper through a sealed tube so nobody else can listen in.

questions: how to use tls with nntp
subtitle: How an NNTP news client and server upgrade a plain connection to an encrypted TLS one with the STARTTLS command.

tldr.problem: NNTP connections were unencrypted, so passwords and articles crossed the network in the clear, and the existing habit of using a separate TCP port (563) for TLS had known drawbacks.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises a STARTTLS capability. A client sends the STARTTLS command, the server answers 382, and TLS negotiation begins on the same connection with the next octet after the response.
tldr.outcome: STARTTLS is the preferred way to use TLS with NNTP. It protects a single link only, and the RFC has since been updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4642 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why NNTP Needs TLS
sections.content:
The Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) moves Netnews articles between clients and servers. The RFC says unencrypted connections were once satisfactory for most purposes, but sending passwords unencrypted is no longer appropriate, and sometimes integrity or confidentiality protection is wanted for the whole connection.

TLS (formerly known as SSL) protects an application protocol from tampering and eavesdropping. The RFC notes that SASL authentication mechanisms can offer a lightweight version of this service, but TLS complements both authentication-only SASL mechanisms and deployed clear-text password login commands.

Some implementations had dedicated TCP port 563 to NNTP over TLS, starting TLS immediately on connect. The RFC discourages this, pointing to the reasons in Section 7 of RFC 2595. Instead it formalizes the STARTTLS command already in occasional use, and calls it the preferred way of using TLS with NNTP.
sections.eli5: Plain NNTP is like talking where anyone nearby can hear. TLS is a way to talk privately. Instead of using a separate private door, this RFC lets you start in the normal room and then switch to private talk.

sections.title: Advertising STARTTLS
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension lists the STARTTLS capability label in its reply to the CAPABILITIES command. The label has no arguments. A server MUST NOT advertise it once a TLS layer is active or after successful authentication. It MAY be advertised before and after a MODE READER command, with the same meaning.

Because the command is about security, a client MUST NOT rely on a cached CAPABILITIES result from an earlier session.
sections.eli5: The server holds up a sign saying 'I can whisper if you like.' Once you are already whispering, the sign comes down, and you should check for the sign again each visit.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Command
sections.content:
The client sends STARTTLS. It MUST NOT be pipelined. The possible replies are 382 (continue with TLS negotiation), 502 (command unavailable, because TLS is already active or authentication has occurred) and 580 (cannot initiate TLS negotiation). The server MUST NOT answer with 480 or 483.

A client MAY use STARTTLS after a 483 reply to another command, which tells it that a secure or encrypted connection is required. It MAY also try it at any time without that prompt, and servers SHOULD accept such requests. After a 580, the server SHOULD refuse later restricted commands with 483, or with 400 followed by closing the connection.

After a 382, the client MUST start TLS before sending any other command. TLS negotiation begins, for both sides, with the first octet after the CRLF of the 382 response. If negotiation fails, both sides SHOULD close the connection, since the session is often left in an indeterminate state.

When the handshake succeeds, NNTP is reset to the state just after the initial greeting, except that the effects of an earlier MODE READER are not reversed. No greeting is sent, so the client speaks next. The server MUST discard what it learned from the client, such as the current newsgroup, and the client MUST NOT rely on what it learned from the server, such as the capability list. A client MUST NOT start TLS if it is already active, and MUST NOT issue MODE READER while TLS is active.

The server stays in the non-authenticated state even if client credentials were supplied during TLS. The AUTHINFO SASL command with the EXTERNAL mechanism MAY be used afterwards to authenticate. Clients SHOULD implement the TLS server_name extension, and so should servers known by several names, so the right certificate can be presented.
sections.eli5: You say 'switch to private mode' and the server says 'okay.' From the very next bit, everything is scrambled. Both of you forget what you said before, because someone could have changed it, and start fresh.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several example sessions. In the main one, a client asks for CAPABILITIES and sees STARTTLS listed. It tries GROUP local.confidential and gets 483 Encryption or stronger authentication required. It sends STARTTLS, receives 382, and TLS negotiation occurs.

Afterwards, the new CAPABILITIES list no longer includes STARTTLS, and the same GROUP command succeeds with 211. A second, inappropriate STARTTLS is answered with 502.

Other examples show a server declining with 580, and a failed negotiation followed by a restricted group request that is refused with 483 and another that gets 400 and a closed connection.
sections.eli5: The examples are like a script: knock, get told the secret room is members-only, switch to private mode, and then walk in. Asking to switch again gets 'you are already private.'

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Everything before the TLS handshake is sent in the clear and can be modified by an active attacker. So clients and servers MUST discard sensitive knowledge gained before the handshake, and SHOULD re-issue CAPABILITIES once TLS is active. Implementations MUST implement the TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5 cipher suite and SHOULD implement TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, so any two compliant implementations can interoperate. All other cipher suites are OPTIONAL.

The protection covers one link only. If an article passes through several servers, encrypting one hop does not make the whole chain private, and authenticating a client to a server does not mean the article was authenticated when the client received it.

The client MUST check the server hostname it used to connect (or the one in the server_name extension) against the identity in the server certificate, and MUST NOT use a name derived from an insecure source such as an insecure DNS lookup. Matching is case-insensitive, a subjectAltName of type dNSName SHOULD be used when present, and a wildcard as the left-most name component MAY be used: a certificate name starting with a wildcard label before .example.com matches a.example.com but not example.com. If matching fails, the client SHOULD ask the user or end the session with QUIT.

An attacker can strip the STARTTLS label from the CAPABILITIES reply, or alter the STARTTLS request and response, to keep a client from using TLS. A client can partly guard against this by remembering that a server offered TLS and raising an alarm if it is missing later.
sections.eli5: Anything said before switching to private mode can be tampered with, so forget it and ask again. Also check that the server's name tag matches who you meant to call, and be suspicious if a server that used to offer private mode suddenly stops.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Status
sections.content:
The RFC gives the formal definition of the extension for the NNTP extension registry. The capability label is STARTTLS with no arguments, and one new command is defined. The command cannot be pipelined, and after it succeeds the STARTTLS and MODE-READER capabilities can no longer be advertised. The change controller is the IESG.

The RFC also defines two new response codes, 382 and 580, both generated by STARTTLS. The ABNF extends the NNTP grammar with starttls-command and starttls-capability, both simply the string STARTTLS.
sections.eli5: This is the paperwork: the new word is written in the official list, along with the two new answer numbers, so everyone uses them the same way.

messages.label: TLS negotiation
messages.note: Traffic is protected from here on.

items.label: Continue with TLS negotiation
items.desc: New in this RFC. TLS starts with the next octet after the CRLF.

items.label: Can not initiate TLS negotiation
items.desc: New in this RFC. The server cannot start TLS, for example because of a configuration or resource problem.

items.label: Command unavailable
items.desc: Returned if a TLS layer is already active or authentication has occurred.

items.label: Secure connection required
items.desc: Returned by other commands; the client MAY then use STARTTLS. Never returned for STARTTLS itself.
